accuracy.evidence: Checked against AQA A level Chemistry specification 7405 section 3.1.7 (oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain, oxidising agents accept electrons, reducing agents donate them, half-equations), OCR A 2.1.5, and NGSS HS-PS1-2. Half-equations Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ and Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ are balanced for atoms and charge, and the series order K Na Ca Mg Al C Zn Fe H Cu Ag Au matches the standard GCSE series. The blast furnace note that CO is the main reductant is correct.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented redox slips: swapping OIL RIG (swap tag and the OIL RIG sort), keeping only the oxygen definition (oxygen tag), calling the oxidising agent the species that is oxidised (agent tag and m2), treating sulfate spectator ions as reacting (spect tag, m7 and the lab label), balancing atoms but not charge (count and side tags, balance step), assuming any metal displaces any other (series tag and copper in magnesium sulfate prediction), and thinking carbon fails on aluminium for cost reasons (cost tag).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagredox is the only lab that drags individual electrons between an iron atom and a copper(II) ion and turns both particles into their products, then adds a charge tally that updates as electrons are added to a half-equation, a reactivity series ladder that highlights the two metals being compared, and a carbon versus electrolysis oxide sort. The shingle gate passed against every other flag lab, including the chemistry labs for ions and reaction types.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sees Fe become Fe²⁺ and Cu²⁺ become Cu only after both electrons move, with each half-equation written as it happens; finds that the electrons' side decides oxidation or reduction; watches the charge readout disagree until exactly 3, 2 and 1 electrons are added; sees copper refuse to displace magnesium on the ladder; and finds aluminium oxide rejected from the carbon box with the reason that aluminium is above carbon.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with a tempting wrong option: that the blue Cu²⁺ ion loses electrons, that Al → Al³⁺ releases one electron per atom, and that copper displaces magnesium because any metal swaps. The lab then moves electrons away from Fe, the charge tally only balances at three electrons, and the ladder shows copper below magnesium, and each done message restates the outcome.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with ten tagged wrong-answer messages (swap, spect, agent, product, count, side, series, oxygen, cost, never). Each message names the specific error and fixes it with the electron rule or the series, for example that the oxidising agent is itself reduced, or that Al³⁺ does gain electrons at the cathode during electrolysis.

readability.evidence: Learner audience. Body paragraphs use short sentences and define each term at first use (half-equation, spectator ion, reducing agent, oxidising agent). The validator readability gate passed for the learner kid and adult targets, and the adult notes name the exam boards and key terms in plain teacher language.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries chemistry: the two definitions, the nail in copper sulfate with its ionic equation, half-equations with charge counts, agent roles and the series, and extraction by carbon or electrolysis. The adult text gives specific slips and teaching moves. The content gate found no filler phrases and explanation overlap stayed under the limit.

mobile.evidence: Reviewed iPhone 13 screenshots of all six steps in light and dark themes. Electrons, balls and labels no longer overlap, the plus and minus electron targets are large squares with the count shown below, the series ladder fits in a narrow column beside the yes or no buttons, and each drag has a full-size button twin below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas aria-label is updated with every spoken message, every drag or tap has a labelled button (move an electron, oxidation or reduction, plus or minus electron, reacts or no reaction, carbon or electrolysis), and axe found no violations in light or dark themes in the walkthrough. Text on tinted tiles uses the main text colour, and copper text is white on dark orange.

OCR (2015, current) A level Chemistry A H432, 2.1.5 Redox
